description: We are a team of students from Kaunas University of Technology (KTU) and members of GIFTed. Our backgrounds are civil engineering, robotics engineering, marketing, architecture, and aviation engineering. We come from very different fields, and that is exactly what we like about working together.
summary:
We built Sharp Navigation, a tool for choosing landing sites on the Moon's south pole using real NASA data. It is a web app that everyone can access. Our website shows a 3D Moon and lets planners compare landing sites side by side.

A good landing site is much more than flat ground. A lander needs sunlight for power and a view of Earth for radio contact. That is why surrounding landscape and project date have to be considered. Our tool combines NASA LOLA height maps, NASA's records of where the Sun and Earth will be, and the skyline around each site. If a launch slips, planners drag the data slider — the tool then suggests a different site or a later landing date. It also checks every site by its worst case, because a lander can miss its target by up to 100 m.

It is relevant because more and more missions are planned to reach the lunar south pole. A bad choice of site can end a mission. That is why our tool is a game-changer — complex data is turned into decisions that anyone can understand.
details:
Sharp Navigation
Sharp Navigation is a browser-based tool designed to help planners choose landing sites near the Moon’s south pole. Users explore a 3D Moon, compare sites, and adjust landing dates to assess sunlight and Earth-communication availability.

The planned scientific analysis combines NASA LOLA elevation maps, Sun and Earth position data, and surrounding terrain. It would suggest alternative sites or dates when schedules change and evaluate worst-case conditions within an assumed 100 m landing uncertainty.

Built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Three.js, and WebGL, the prototype requires no installation or specialized hardware. Its creative approach connects location and timing in one visual workflow, turning complex information into understandable comparisons.

We considered power availability, radio contact, terrain obstructions, changing dates, landing uncertainty, usability for everyday users, and the needs of technical staff. Our intended impact is to support clearer early planning for lunar exploration. The current prototype demonstrates the workflow using NASA imagery and labelled simulated indicators; validated scientific calculations remain a development goal.
